title: Find Median from Data Stream
description: Maintain a running median over a growing stream of numbers, using two balanced heaps split at the median.

blocks.text: Design a MedianFinder class supporting addNum(num), which adds a number from a data stream, and findMedian(), which returns the median of all numbers added so far.

blocks.caption: Two balanced heaps split the stream into a lower half and an upper half, meeting exactly at the median.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["addNum(num)","Adds a number to the running data stream"],["findMedian()","Returns the median of all numbers added so far"],["Goal","Both operations should be efficient, since the stream can be very long"]]}

blocks.text: Maintaining a running median of a growing stream is the classic two-heap pattern: a max-heap holds the smaller half of the numbers, a min-heap holds the larger half, and keeping their sizes within one of each other guarantees the median sits exactly at the boundary between them, readable in O(1).

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This two-heap "balanced halves" idea is the same one behind Design Front Middle Back Queue's two-deque split, just using heaps (for value-based ordering) instead of deques (for position-based ordering).

Picture a seesaw with two piles: the lower half of all numbers seen so far on one side, the upper half on the other, kept balanced in size (differing by at most one). The median is always readable directly from the boundary: either the top of the larger pile (odd total count) or the average of both piles' tops (even total count).

blocks.caption: A balanced split keeps the median exactly at the boundary between the two piles.

items: small (a max-heap) holds the lower half of numbers; large (a min-heap) holds the upper half.
On adding a number, push it to the appropriate half based on comparison with small's top, then rebalance if one heap grows more than one larger than the other.
findMedian reads directly from the heap top(s): if small is larger, its top is the median; otherwise, average both tops.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The medians returned are 1.5 then 2.0, matching the expected output exactly. After adding 3, small holds {1,2} and large holds {3}; since small has one more element, its top (2) is the median.
A direct approach stores every number in a list and sorts it fresh every time findMedian is called. This is correct and simple but re-sorts the entire growing list on every single query.

Maintaining two balanced heaps keeps the data always "half-sorted enough" to read the median instantly: addNum only needs O(log n) to insert and possibly rebalance, and findMedian is O(1), since the boundary between the two heaps is always exactly where the median sits.
Store every number in a list. On findMedian, sort a copy of the list and read the middle value(s) directly.

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Re-sorting the entire stream on every findMedian call is wasteful, especially with many interleaved queries on a long stream.

Maintain two heaps: small (a max-heap) for the lower half, large (a min-heap) for the upper half, kept within one element of each other in size. On addNum, insert into the correct half based on comparison with small's current top, then rebalance if needed by moving one element between heaps. findMedian reads directly from the heap top(s) in O(1).

items: addNum: push to small if empty or num <= small's top, else push to large; then rebalance if sizes differ by more than 1.
Rebalancing moves at most one element between heaps, O(log n).
findMedian: O(1), reading small's top alone (odd total) or averaging both tops (even total).

items: A running median over a growing stream is the classic two-balanced-heaps pattern: a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half.
Keeping heap sizes within one of each other guarantees the median is always readable directly from the heap tops, no scanning needed.
This structure supports insertion in O(log n) and median queries in O(1), a strong improvement over re-sorting on every query.

blocks.text: Find Median from Data Stream is solved with two balanced heaps, a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept within one element of each other in size. This lets addNum run in O(log n) and findMedian in O(1), since the median always sits exactly at the boundary between the two heaps.
